--- title: "A scenario grid" --- The district has to decide what to put in the next distribution. Five options are on the table: 1. **Withdraw the nets.** There is no campaign at all. This is not a serious policy, but it is the counterfactual every other option is measured against. It is also the arm that results if the campaign is not restated. 2. **Replace like for like** with pyrethroid-only nets at the same 0.70 coverage. 3. **Switch to PBO**, again at 0.70. 4. **Switch to pyrrole**, again at 0.70. 5. **PBO plus IRS at 0.60 plus LSM at 0.30.** This is the most expensive package. Every arm shares the same setting (prevalence 0.45, resistance 0.30, pyrethroid-only nets at 0.70 now) and therefore the same `EirTarget`. The baseline EIR is inverted from the same prevalence under the same current net mix. All five scenarios therefore start from an identical transmission intensity and an identical pre-campaign trajectory. Any difference between them is caused by the campaign and nothing else. ## Building the grid The shared fields go in a dictionary and are splatted into each `Scenario`. Only the campaign is written out per arm. ::: {#30bef6ed .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import run_scenarios from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget district = dict( res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, py_only=0.70, # the nets in place today routine=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"), ) grid = [ Scenario(name="Withdraw", **district), Scenario( name="Pyrethroid-only", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only", **district, ), Scenario( name="PBO", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", **district, ), Scenario( name="Pyrrole", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pyrrole", **district, ), Scenario( name="PBO + IRS + LSM", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", irs_future=0.60, lsm=0.30, **district, ), ] len(grid) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5 ``` ::: ::: If R is your first language, the dictionary-splat idiom is the Python equivalent of `do.call(Scenario, c(district, list(name = "PBO", ...)))`. Use it rather than repeating the shared fields five times over. A typo in one arm's `Q0` would silently break the comparison. ## One call `run_scenarios` takes the list, loads the models once, and puts the five scenarios through the emulator as a single batch. Five arms cost barely more than one. ::: {#3d3cecee .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} res = run_scenarios(grid) res.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (5, 23) ``` ::: ::: What comes back is five rows, one per arm, and the same twenty-three columns as before. ## The shared baseline Check it before reading anything else. If the five arms did not start from the same place, none of the comparisons that follow would mean anything. ::: {#6cfcf8a7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[["name", "dn0_use", "itn_use", "eir_baseline", "prev_y9"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
name dn0_use itn_use eir_baseline prev_y9
0 Withdraw 0.311 0.7 31.960129 0.456028
1 Pyrethroid-only 0.311 0.7 31.960129 0.456028
2 PBO 0.311 0.7 31.960129 0.456028
3 Pyrrole 0.311 0.7 31.960129 0.456028
4 PBO + IRS + LSM 0.311 0.7 31.960129 0.456028
``` ::: ::: All five arms share the same `dn0_use`, the same `itn_use`, an `eir_baseline` of about 32 infectious bites per person per year, and a `prev_y9` of about 0.456 against the 0.45 that went in. They are indistinguishable up to the campaign. They diverge only after it. ## The summary table The campaign columns and the two endline outcomes are what the grid was built for. ::: {#acdd410b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} res[[ "name", "net_future", "dn0_future", "itn_future", "irs_future", "lsm", "prev_endline", "cases_endline", ]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
name net_future dn0_future itn_future irs_future lsm prev_endline cases_endline
0 Withdraw none 0.00000 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.498149 2.127164
1 Pyrethroid-only pyrethroid_only 0.31100 0.7 0.0 0.0 0.483688 2.433113
2 PBO pyrethroid_pbo 0.48495 0.7 0.0 0.0 0.470118 2.412444
3 Pyrrole pyrethroid_pyrrole 0.55015 0.7 0.0 0.0 0.464200 2.389937
4 PBO + IRS + LSM pyrethroid_pbo 0.48495 0.7 0.6 0.3 0.038096 0.165287
``` ::: ::: Read the `dn0_future` column first. At resistance 0.30 a pyrethroid-only net kills about 0.31 of the mosquitoes that touch it, a PBO net about 0.48, and a pyrrole net about 0.55. The ranking of the three net arms follows from that ordering and nothing else, since every other covariate is held fixed. The combination arm has the PBO `dn0_future` (the nets are the same nets) but adds spraying at 0.60 and larviciding at 0.30 on top. The endline prevalence it reaches is an order of magnitude below any net-only arm. Within nets, the product choice changes prevalence by a few points. Adding a second and third vector-control measure changes it considerably further. Whether the district can afford that is not a question the emulator answers. ## The withdrawal arm The first row of the grid shows the values the defaults produce. ::: {#51b3f2b8 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} res.loc[res["name"] == "Withdraw", ["net_future", "dn0_future", "itn_future", "irs_future"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
net_future dn0_future itn_future irs_future
0 none 0.0 0.0 0.0
``` ::: ::: `net_future` is `"none"`, `dn0_future` is 0, and `itn_future` is 0. That row was built by passing the district dictionary and nothing else, with no `itn_future` and no `net_type_future`. Those are the values the defaults supply. If the campaign is not restated, the district has been modelled as stopping net distribution altogether. No warning is raised. The call succeeds, the frame comes back, and the trajectory is plausible. The only indication is the rebound, and it is obviously wrong only to a reader who was expecting the nets to continue. ::: {#3c74fe2f .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np withdraw = res.loc[res["name"] == "Withdraw"].iloc[0] like_for_like = res.loc[res["name"] == "Pyrethroid-only"].iloc[0] float(withdraw["prev_endline"]), float(like_for_like["prev_endline"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (0.49814853072166443, 0.4836880564689636) ``` ::: ::: Here the withdrawal arm ends about one and a half prevalence points above like-for-like replacement. The gap is small enough to be mistaken for noise by a reader who was not looking for it. The difference in cumulative case burden between the two is considerably larger, as [Comparing campaigns](comparing.qmd) works out. Keep the arm deliberately. It is the counterfactual that makes "cases averted" a meaningful quantity. ## Next - [Comparing campaigns](comparing.qmd) — rank the five arms and count the cases averted. - [Exporting results](exporting.qmd) — get the grid out of Python. - [Nets and dn0](../04-estimint/nets-and-dn0.qmd) — the resistance curves behind `dn0_future`.
